11788 — Zayd ibn Thābit narrated:
“We were in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ arranging the Qur’an from written pieces of parchment.”
Authentic: Narrated by al-Tirmidhī (3954), whose wording is cited here, Aḥmad (21606, 21607), authenticated by Ibn Ḥibbān (7304), al-Ḥākim (2/229), and al-Bayhaqī in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah (7/147).
Al-Bayhaqī said:
“This appears to mean arranging the revealed portions of the Book: placing the separately revealed verses into their respective sūrahs and gathering them therein according to the directions of the Prophet ﷺ, while they were also preserved in the hearts.”
The Second Stage
Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, then instructed Zayd ibn Thābit to gather the Qur’an into a single muṣḥaf according to one mode: the dialect of Quraysh.
He relied upon the portions written during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ upon pieces of parchment, shoulder blades, and palm stalks, which had been preserved in the household of the Prophet ﷺ, as well as what was preserved in the memories of the people and agreed with those written materials.
He gathered them into one muṣḥaf after the Battle of al-Yamāmah for the reason previously mentioned.
The completion of this work took approximately one year. The Battle of al-Yamāmah occurred during the eleventh year and the beginning of the twelfth year after the Hijrah, while al-Ṣiddīq died in the thirteenth year. The period between them was therefore approximately one year.
This copy then passed to the succeeding caliph, the Commander of the Believers ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him. Afterward, it remained with the Mother of the Believers Ḥafṣah bint ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with them both.
It is certain that this copy had its verses and sūrahs arranged in the order in which the Prophet ﷺ used to recite them during the prayers.
The reports concerning the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ in prayer, which are cited in their proper places in al-Jāmiʿ al-Kāmil, demonstrate that his recitation followed the same order found in the muṣḥaf presently in our hands.
Whenever he occasionally recited in a different sequence, the Companions explicitly reported it. For this reason, the majority of scholars permitted reciting the Qur’an, whether during prayer or outside it, in an order different from the sequence of the sūrahs, by placing one before another. However, they considered doing so contrary to what is preferable.
The Prophet ﷺ likewise reviewed the Qur’an with Gabriel, peace be upon him, in its arranged order twice during the year in which he died.
This is established in the agreed-upon hadith of Fāṭimah, in which the Prophet ﷺ spoke privately to her and said:
“Gabriel used to review the Qur’an with me once every year, but this year he reviewed it with me twice. I do not think this means anything except that my appointed time has arrived…”
The noble Companions received the Qur’an from him according to this arrangement.
As for the claim that the arrangement of the sūrahs within the muṣḥaf resulted from the independent judgment of the Companions, this requires examination.
The question naturally arises: How did the Prophet ﷺ conduct his final two reviews of the Qur’an with Gabriel, peace be upon him? Were the verses and sūrahs not arranged during those reviews?
Furthermore, how did Abū Bakr compile the Qur’an? Were its verses and sūrahs not arranged?
It is therefore self-evident that the muṣḥaf was arranged. ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, may Allah be pleased with him, adopted it in that same form, and it is the muṣḥaf presently in our hands.
It has authentically been reported from Samurah that he said:
“The Qur’an was reviewed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on several occasions, and they would say: ‘This recitation of ours follows the final review.’”
It was narrated by al-Bazzār and al-Ḥākim with an authentic chain, as previously mentioned.
The words “they would say” refer to the Companions.
ʿAbīdah al-Salmānī said:
“The recitation that was reviewed with the Prophet ﷺ during the year in which he died is the recitation that the people recite today.”
Narrated by Ibn Abī Shaybah (30922) through Ibn Sīrīn from him.
Ibn Sīrīn said:
“Gabriel used to review the Qur’an with the Prophet ﷺ during every month of Ramadan. During the year in which the Prophet ﷺ died, Gabriel reviewed it with him twice.”
He then said:
“It is therefore hoped that this recitation of ours follows the final review.”
See: Sunan Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, The Book of Tafsīr (1/239, no. 57).
Al-Baghawī said in Sharḥ al-Sunnah (4/526):
“Zayd ibn Thābit witnessed the final review during which what had been abrogated and what remained were clarified. He wrote it for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and recited it back to him. He continued teaching the people according to it until he died. For this reason, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar relied upon him for its compilation, and ʿUthmān appointed him to copy the muṣḥafs.”
On the basis of what has been established, the reports found in some books on the sciences of the Qur’an claiming that ʿUthmān personally arranged the sūrahs are incorrect, because they are later reports unsupported by any statement from the Companions or the Successors.
The fact that the personal muṣḥafs of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿūd, and others differed in their ordering from the muṣḥaf of ʿUthmān does not prove that the arrangement of the sūrahs resulted from ʿUthmān’s independent judgment.
Those Companions wrote their personal copies according to whatever arrangement was convenient for them.
For example, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib wrote his sheets according to the chronological order of revelation. They began with:
“Read,”
then:
“O you who are wrapped up,”
then:
“Nūn,”
and continued in that manner through the Makkan revelations, followed by the Madinan revelations.
All of it was the Qur’an, whether Sūrat al-Nisāʾ was placed before Sūrat Āl ʿImrān or after it.
Some of them also omitted certain sūrahs because they believed those sūrahs were not part of the Qur’an. Their personal copies sometimes contained explanations of certain verses as well.
It is also possible that they had not examined the copy written by Zayd ibn Thābit for Abū Bakr according to the final review, because neither Ubayy ibn Kaʿb nor ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd was a member of the committee appointed by ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, to copy the standard muṣḥaf.
The Third Stage
During the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, personal copies of the Qur’an became numerous.
ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd possessed a muṣḥaf from which he dictated to the people of Kūfah. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb had a muṣḥaf, as did ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad, Sālim the freed slave of Abū Ḥudhayfah, and other Companions.
They dictated from these copies to their students and companions.
These personal muṣḥafs differed in some of their modes of recitation because the Qur’an had been revealed in seven modes as an ease for the Muslims.
This became one of the reasons for unifying the muṣḥaf upon a single mode, in order to remove the disagreement that had arisen among the Muslims.
When this disagreement intensified, people began declaring one another mistaken, the situation worsened, and discord was feared.
The Commander of the Believers ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, may Allah be pleased with him, therefore gathered the Muslims to consult them concerning the matter. This occurred around the twenty-fifth year after the Hijrah.
Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said in his biography of Zayd ibn Thābit in al-Istīʿāb:
“When the people differed in recitation during the caliphate of ʿUthmān, his judgment and that of the Companions agreed that the Qur’an should be returned to one mode.
He selected the mode preserved by Zayd—that is, the copy which Zayd had written for Abū Bakr and which was then in the possession of Ḥafṣah.
He instructed Zayd to dictate the muṣḥaf to a group of men from Quraysh whom he had assembled. It was written in the form presently held by the people. The reports concerning this are mass-transmitted in meaning, even though their individual wordings differ.”
End quote.
Several copies were produced during the caliphate of ʿUthmān. The reports differ concerning their exact number.
The soundest reports state that there were five, while the highest reported number is seven.
ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, sent them to six cities: Makkah, Syria, Bahrain, Yemen, Kūfah, and Baṣrah. He retained one copy in Madinah.
He ordered that every separate portion or personal muṣḥaf held by some of the Companions be burned, and the people hastened to comply with his command.
Ibn Abī Dāwūd narrated in Kitāb al-Maṣāḥif (1/187) from Muṣʿab ibn Saʿd, who said:
“I witnessed the people in great numbers when ʿUthmān burned the muṣḥafs, and they approved of what he did.”
He also said:
“No one among them objected to it.”
An exception is what has been reported concerning Ibn Masʿūd: that he initially did not carry out ʿUthmān’s instruction and instead told his students to preserve the muṣḥaf they possessed.
Allah then guided him to return to the judgment of ʿUthmān, which was in reality the judgment of the entire Muslim community.
Nevertheless, other recitations transmitted from Ibn Masʿūd spread through the narrations of his students and were preserved in books of tafsīr and hadith.
All later muṣḥafs were copied from these ʿUthmānic muṣḥafs as the territory of the Islamic state expanded.
The Muslims therefore reached consensus upon the muṣḥaf presently in existence, which was copied from the ʿUthmānic muṣḥafs according to one mode. The ʿUthmānic muṣḥaf became the authoritative standard for all Muslims.
Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī said:
“The entirety of the Qur’an revealed by Allah, the Exalted, which He commanded to be preserved, and whose ruling or recitation He did not abrogate, is that which exists between the two covers and is contained within the muṣḥaf of ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him.
Nothing has been omitted from it, and nothing has been added to it. Each succeeding generation transmitted it from the preceding generation, and it is the miracle of the Messenger, peace be upon him.”
End quote.
See: Nukat al-Intiṣār (p. 59).
The Orthography of the Muṣḥaf
The orthographic style used in writing the muṣḥaf was the form of writing known among the Arabs at that time. Rules of spelling were formulated later. However, the early scholars prohibited rewriting the muṣḥaf according to the newly developed spelling conventions.
Imām Mālik was asked:
“What is your view regarding someone who commissions a muṣḥaf to be written today? Should it be written according to the spelling conventions newly introduced by the people?”
He replied:
“I do not consider that appropriate. Rather, it should be written according to the original script.”
Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, who died in 444 AH, said after mentioning the preceding opinion of Mālik:
“None of the scholars of the Muslim community disagreed with him concerning that.”
See: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Maʿrifat Marsūm Maṣāḥif Ahl al-Amṣār (pp. 9–10).
It has been related that Imām Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said:
“It is forbidden to depart from the official muṣḥaf in the writing of a wāw, a yāʾ, an alif, or anything else.”
Al-Bayhaqī said in Shuʿab al-Īmān (4/219):
“Whoever writes a muṣḥaf should preserve the orthography with which they wrote those muṣḥafs. He should neither differ from them in it nor alter anything that they wrote. They possessed greater knowledge, were more truthful in heart and speech, and were more trustworthy than we are. We should not imagine that we can correct them or find fault with them.”
Al-Zamakhsharī, who died in 538 AH, said that in the written form of the verse:
“And they say, ‘What is the matter with this Messenger that he eats food?’”
 [Sūrat al-Furqān 25:7]
the preposition lām was written separately. It appears in this way despite departing from ordinary Arabic writing conventions, because the script of the muṣḥaf is an established practice that must not be altered.
The Muslims have continued to follow this practice until the present day. The opposition of anyone who differs from them carries no consideration.
As for placing dots in the Qur’an, no objection to it has been transmitted from any of the early Muslims. Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn, and others were asked about it, and they said:
“There is no harm in it.”
Al-Bayhaqī transmitted in Shuʿab al-Īmān (4/219) from al-Ḥalīmī:
“The dots themselves are not recited, such that something which is not Qur’an might be imagined to be Qur’an because of them. They are merely signs indicating how the written text is to be pronounced. There is therefore no harm in adding them for those who need them.”
The Qur’anic Recitations
It is incorrect to believe that the seven famous recitations known today are what is meant by the seven modes mentioned in the hadith:
“The Qur’an was revealed in seven modes.”
The ʿUthmānic muṣḥaf was standardized upon one mode, namely the dialect of Quraysh.
The recognized recitations are not restricted to seven. The mass-transmitted recitations number ten, while Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām, Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī, and Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭabarī mentioned even more than that.
The existence of multiple recitations was known during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ. He received them from his Lord through Gabriel, peace be upon him. The copies of the ʿUthmānic muṣḥaf were written in a manner that accommodated these recitations.
The people of each region recited according to what they had received from the Companions and Successors, provided that the recitation agreed with the written form of the muṣḥaf.
Some recitations did not conform to that written form. When the Companions reached consensus upon the ʿUthmānic muṣḥaf, those recitations were regarded as anomalous.
It is also incorrect to say that the mass-transmitted recitations originated from the ʿUthmānic script. The ʿUthmānic script does not produce a recitation; rather, it serves as one of the criteria by which a recitation is evaluated.
The reason later scholars focused upon seven recitations is that the narrators transmitting from the leading reciters were numerous. When people’s determination weakened, scholars selected from the recitations conforming to the written muṣḥaf those that were easiest to preserve and through which recitation could be accurately regulated.
Al-Suyūṭī transmitted from Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib al-Qaysī:
“Before Ibn Mujāhid, who died in 324 AH, Ibn Jubayr al-Makkī authored a work on the recitations in which he limited himself to five, selecting one leading reciter from each region.
He limited them to five because ʿUthmān had sent five muṣḥafs to those regions. It is also said that he sent seven: those five, one to Yemen, and one to Bahrain.
Since no report was later heard concerning the two muṣḥafs sent to Yemen and Bahrain, Ibn Mujāhid and others wished to preserve the number corresponding to the muṣḥafs. They therefore substituted two reciters for the muṣḥafs of Bahrain and Yemen, thereby completing the number.
This coincidentally matched the number mentioned in the report. Those who did not understand the origin of the issue and lacked insight consequently assumed that the seven modes meant the seven recitations.
The fundamental criteria are an authentic chain of oral transmission, conformity with a valid aspect of Arabic, and agreement with the written script.”
End quote.
Cited from al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān (2/527).
The fame of the seven reciters is due to Ibn Mujāhid’s book al-Sabʿah.
Thus, when al-Baghawī mentioned in the introduction to his tafsīr, Maʿālim al-Tanzīl, the recitations of Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd, Ḥamzah ibn Ḥabīb al-Zayyāt, Abū al-Ḥasan al-Kisāʾī, and Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Ḥaḍramī al-Baṣrī—nine reciters in total—he said:
“I have mentioned the recitations of these men because there is agreement upon the permissibility of reciting according to them.”
The hadith scholars played a prominent role in preserving the famous recitations through authentic, uninterrupted chains leading back to the Prophet ﷺ.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, described him by saying:
“He does not speak from his own desire. It is nothing but revelation sent down.”
 [Sūrat al-Najm 53:3–4]
And He said:
“Recite what has been revealed to you from the Book of your Lord. None can change His words, and you will never find any refuge apart from Him.”
 [Sūrat al-Kahf 18:27]
They therefore made the authenticity of the chain of transmission one of the conditions for accepting a recitation. Consequently, they prohibited reciting on the basis of analogy or personal reasoning.
Ibn al-Jazarī, who died in 833 AH, said in al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr (1/46):
“The seven recitations specified by al-Shāṭibī, together with the three recitations of Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb, and Khalaf, are mass-transmitted and necessarily known as part of the religion.
Every reading uniquely transmitted by one of the ten is necessarily known as having been revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. No one disputes any of this except an ignorant person.”
Among the principal reciters after the generation of the Companions were:
In Madinah: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, Muʿādh ibn al-Ḥārith, and Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī.
In Makkah: ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and ʿIkrimah.
In Kūfah: ʿAlqamah, al-Shaʿbī, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.
In Baṣrah: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ibn Sīrīn, and Qatādah.
In Syria: al-Mughīrah ibn Abī Shihāb al-Makhzūmī, a companion of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.
Through these authorities, the recitations spread until they reached the later reciters through uninterrupted chains of transmission.
This is demonstrated by the report that al-Aṣmaʿī asked Abū ʿAmr al-Baṣrī, who died in 154 AH, about two verses in Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt whose written forms could not by themselves determine the pronunciation:
“And We left for him among later generations.”
 [Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt 37:78]
And:
“And We blessed him and Isaac.”
 [Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt 37:113]
He asked him:
“How is their correct pronunciation known?”
Abū ʿAmr replied:
“It can only be known by hearing it from the earliest teachers.”
See: Ibn Mujāhid, al-Qirāʾāt al-Sabʿ (p. 48).
Ten reciters became especially famous:
Nāfiʿ and Abū Jaʿfar in Madinah;
Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb in Baṣrah;
ʿAbdullāh ibn Kathīr in Makkah;
ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿĀmir in Syria;
ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisāʾī in Kūfah;
and Khalaf ibn Hishām in Baghdad.
Brief Biographies of the Ten Reciters
1. Ibn ʿĀmir al-Shāmī
He was ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Yazīd ibn Tamīm, known by the kunyah Abū ʿAmr.
He studied the Qur’an under a number of Companions, including Muʿāwiyah, Faḍālah ibn ʿUbayd, and Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ. He also transmitted from ʿUthmān through al-Mughīrah ibn Abī Shihāb al-Makhzūmī.
ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān and some of these Companions had recited directly to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
Ibn ʿĀmir died in 118 AH, and many students learned from him.
2. Ibn Kathīr al-Makkī
He was ʿAbdullāh ibn Kathīr ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn Zādhān ibn Fayrūz ibn Hurmuz, a Persian from Makkah.
He was born in Makkah in 45 AH and met the Companions Anas ibn Mālik, ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr, and Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī.
He studied under Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. They studied under Ibn ʿAbbās, who recited to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Zayd ibn Thābit, both of whom transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
He died in 120 AH.
3. ʿĀṣim
He was ʿĀṣim ibn Bahdalah, Abū al-Najūd al-Khayyāṭ al-Asadī al-Kūfī.
He studied under Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh. They studied under ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Zayd ibn Thābit, and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, all of whom recited to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
He became the leading reciter of Kūfah and died in 128 AH.
His most famous transmitters included:
Shuʿbah ibn ʿAyyāsh al-Asadī al-Nahshalī al-Kūfī, who was born in 95 AH, became a leading authority and proof in recitation, and died in 192 AH.
Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān ibn al-Mughīrah ibn Abī Dāwūd al-Asadī al-Kūfī, who was born in 90 AH, was among the most knowledgeable students of ʿĀṣim, and died in 180 AH.
4. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ al-Baṣrī
He was Zabbān ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn ʿAmmār ibn al-ʿUryān al-Māzinī al-Tamīmī.
He was born in 68 AH and studied under several Successors, including Mujāhid ibn Jabr, ʿAṭāʾ, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and ʿIkrimah, the freed slave of Ibn ʿAbbās.
They studied under ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, who recited to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who recited to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
Abū ʿAmr al-Baṣrī also studied under many other teachers. Ibn al-Jazarī said that none of the seven reciters had more teachers than he did.
He was the leading authority and reciter of Baṣrah and died in 154 AH.
5. Ḥamzah al-Kūfī
He was Ḥamzah ibn Ḥabīb ibn ʿImārah al-Zayyāt, the client of ʿIkrimah ibn Rabīʿ al-Taymī.
He became the leading reciter of Kūfah after ʿĀṣim.
He studied under Sulaymān ibn Mihrān al-Aʿmash, who transmitted from Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, from Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, from ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, and Ibn Masʿūd, who had recited to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
Leading scholars of Kūfah studied under him, including Sufyān al-Thawrī and Wakīʿ.
He died in 188 AH.
6. Nāfiʿ al-Madanī
He was Nāfiʿ ibn Abī Nuʿaym, the client of Jaʿūnah. He was originally from Isfahan, was dark-skinned, and lived a long life.
He studied under seventy Successors, who had studied under Abū Hurayrah, Ibn ʿAbbās, and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿah. All of them transmitted through Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who recited to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
Nāfiʿ became the leading authority in recitation in Madinah.
He was born in 70 AH. Mālik and others studied under him. He died in 169 AH.
Among his most famous students were:
Qālūn, who was ʿĪsā ibn Mīnā ibn Wardān, the reciter of Madinah. Qālūn was a title given to him by Nāfiʿ because of the excellence of his recitation. He was born in 120 AH and died in 220 AH.
Warsh, who was ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Miṣrī. Warsh was a title given to him because of the brightness of his complexion. Leadership in recitation in Egypt passed to him. He was born in 120 AH and died in 197 AH.
7. Al-Kisāʾī al-Kūfī
He was ʿAlī ibn Ḥamzah, the grammarian, of Persian origin.
He was born in 119 AH and died in 189 AH. He was called al-Kisāʾī because he entered the state of pilgrimage consecration while wearing a cloak.
He was one of the leading reciters and the foremost grammarian of Kūfah.
He studied under Abū ʿImārah Ḥamzah ibn Ḥabīb al-Zayyāt, who studied under Sulaymān ibn Mihrān, from Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, from Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān and ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, both of whom recited to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
His most famous transmitters included:
Al-Layth ibn Khālid al-Marwazī al-Baghdādī, who died in 240 AH.
Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Dūrī al-Baghdādī, the leading teacher of reciters. He recited to al-Kisāʾī according to his transmission and to Yaḥyā al-Yazīdī according to the recitation of Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ al-Baṣrī.
He lived a long life, authored works on the recitations, was born sometime in the 150s AH, and died in 246 AH.
There are three additional reciters whose recitations were also recognized as mass-transmitted, bringing the total to ten. Ibn al-Jazarī, who died in 833 AH, authored al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr concerning them.
8. Abū Jaʿfar
He was Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ al-Makhzūmī al-Madanī, one of the ten reciters.
He studied under ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah, who transmitted from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
He died in 130 AH.
His most famous transmitters were:
Ibn Wardān, ʿĪsā ibn Wardān al-Madanī, one of the foremost and earliest students associated with Nāfiʿ. He died in 160 AH.
Ibn Jammāz, Sulaymān ibn Muḥammad ibn Muslim al-Zuhrī al-Madanī, who died in 170 AH.
9. Yaʿqūb al-Baṣrī
He was Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq ibn Yazīd al-Ḥaḍramī al-Baṣrī, one of the ten reciters.
He was born in 117 AH and died in 205 AH.
He studied under Abū ʿAmr al-Baṣrī, who transmitted from Mujāhid ibn Jabr and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who studied under ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, who recited to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who recited to the Prophet ﷺ.
His most famous transmitters were:
Ruways, Muḥammad ibn al-Mutawakkil al-Luʾluʾī al-Baṣrī, who died in 238 AH.
Rawḥ, Rawḥ ibn ʿAbd al-Muʾmin al-Hudhalī al-Baṣrī, the grammarian, who died in 235 AH.
10. Khalaf
He was Khalaf ibn Hishām al-Bazzār al-Baghdādī, one of the ten reciters.
He was born in 150 AH and died in 229 AH.
He studied under Yaḥyā ibn Sulaym, who studied under Ḥamzah ibn ʿImārah ibn Ismāʿīl, who transmitted from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from al-Minhāl ibn ʿAmr, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
His most famous transmitters were:
Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUthmān al-Marwazī al-Baghdādī al-Warrāq, who died in 286 AH.
Idrīs ibn ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Ḥaddād al-Baghdādī, who was born in 189 AH and died in 292 AH.
Ibn Mujāhid—Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn Mūsā ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn Mujāhid al-Baghdādī, who died in 324 AH—authored his famous book al-Sabʿah on this subject.
He included ʿAlī ibn Ḥamzah al-Kisāʾī rather than Yaʿqūb al-Baṣrī. Their recitations consequently became famous throughout the regions. Some scholars later added the remaining three reciters, bringing the total to ten.
The reciters who learned from these authorities then became exceedingly numerous throughout the Muslim lands and cannot be counted. Their chains of transmission have continued uninterrupted until the present day.
This is a unique distinction of the Noble Qur’an and did not occur for any previous revealed scripture.
The wisdom behind it is that Allah made this Book a beacon of guidance until the Day of Resurrection and guaranteed its preservation from distortion and alteration.
The scholars of recitation authored valuable works on the Qur’anic recitations. Among the most important are:
al-Tadhkirah by Ibn Abī Ghalbūn al-Ḥalabī, who died in 399 AH;
al-Tabṣirah by al-Qayrawānī, who died in 437 AH;
and al-Taysīr by Abū ʿAmr ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Dānī, who died in 444 AH;
as well as many other works.
They established three conditions for accepting a recitation.
Ibn al-Jazarī said:
“Every recitation that conforms to Arabic, even according to one valid linguistic interpretation; agrees with one of the ʿUthmānic muṣḥafs, even by reasonable possibility; and possesses an authentic chain of transmission, is a sound recitation that may not be rejected and whose denial is unlawful.”
I say: All ten famous recitations are accommodated by the ʿUthmānic script.
Whenever one of these three conditions is absent, the recitation is anomalous, even if its chain of transmission is authentic.
An example is the report narrated by al-Bukhārī in al-Tafsīr (4943) and Muslim in The Prayer of Travelers (824/282), from ʿAlqamah:
I entered Syria with a group of the companions of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd. Abū al-Dardāʾ heard of our arrival and came to us.
He asked:
“Is there anyone among you who can recite?”
We replied:
“Yes.”
He asked:
“Which of you is the most proficient?”
They pointed to me.
He said:
“Recite.”
I recited:
“By the night when it covers, and by the day when it appears, and by the male and the female.”
He asked:
“Did you hear this directly from the mouth of your teacher?”
I replied:
“Yes.”
He said:
“I too heard it directly from the mouth of the Prophet ﷺ, but these people reject our recitation.”
Another wording states that Abū al-Dardāʾ said:
“I testify that I heard the Prophet ﷺ recite it in this manner, while these people want me to recite:
‘And by Him who created the male and the female.’
By Allah, I will not follow them.”
Another example is the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, who said:
“The Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught me to recite:
‘Indeed, I am the Provider, the Possessor of power, the Firm.’”
This relates to the established verse:
“Indeed, Allah alone is the Provider, the Possessor of power, the Firm.”
 [Sūrat al-Dhāriyāt 51:58]
Narrated by Abū Dāwūd (3993), al-Tirmidhī (2940), and Aḥmad (3741). Its chain is authentic. Al-Tirmidhī said:
“This is a good authentic hadith.”
These recitations, despite the authenticity of their chains, are anomalous because they differ from the general recitation circulated among the other Companions and are not accommodated by the ʿUthmānic script.
No one may recite in either an obligatory or voluntary prayer anything other than what is contained in the muṣḥaf upon which consensus has been established.
Mālik, may Allah have mercy upon him, said regarding a person who recites in prayer according to a reading attributed to Ibn Masʿūd or another Companion that differs from the muṣḥaf:
“Prayer should not be performed behind him.”
Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr transmitted the consensus of the Muslims that anomalous recitations may not be recited and that one should not pray behind a person who recites according to them.
See: al-Burhān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān (1/333).
Ibn Ḥazm said in Jawāmiʿ al-Sīrah (p. 271), after listing the well-known reciters previously mentioned:
“There are also other recitations transmitted from famous authorities which did not become widely established from them. It is not lawful to recite according to them as a formal recitation, to use them in prayer, or to write them in the muṣḥafs at all.”
I say: There was once disagreement concerning this issue, but that disagreement ended with this consensus. Al-Nawawī and others likewise reported consensus concerning it.
It is likewise impermissible to attribute to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as Qur’an anything other than what is contained within the muṣḥaf upon which consensus has been established.
There is no objection, however, to transmitting in works of tafsīr and hadith other reports attributed to Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and others that differ from the ʿUthmānic muṣḥaf, in order to use them as supporting evidence for the meaning of a Qur’anic verse.
Their ruling nevertheless remains that of anomalous recitations. They may therefore not be testified to as the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. That designation is restricted to what is contained within the ʿUthmānic muṣḥaf.
The Arabic script remained without dots and vowel markings from the era in which revelation was written.
When Islam spread beyond the Arabian Peninsula into non-Arab lands and correct recitation of the Qur’an became difficult for non-Arabs, the need arose for dots and vowel markings.
Most reports indicate that Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī—Ẓālim ibn ʿAmr ibn Sufyān, who died in 69 AH and was born during the prophetic era—was the first to place reading marks in the muṣḥafs.
He had recited the Qur’an to ʿUthmān and ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is therefore most likely that his system of marking corresponded to the recitation of ʿUthmān and ʿAlī, although the written form of the muṣḥaf continued to accommodate the other famous recitations.
There were many reasons for introducing dots and vowel markings. The reports generally agree that grammatical and pronunciation errors had appeared in Arabic speech and in the recitation of the Noble Qur’an.
The Muslims throughout the eastern and western lands therefore agreed upon reading the Qur’an according to a regulated and consistent method.
